title: What's so important about legal precedent?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain legal precedent (stare decisis) and its role in common law systems. They trace common law to Henry II in 1154, contrast common law with civil law, and cover Justice Brandeis's 1932 Burnett v. Coronado Oil and Gas dissent. They list factors for overturning precedent (Constitution vs. statutory law, workability, reliance, abandonment, legitimacy, was it close, quality of reasoning, changed facts), and debate originalism versus pragmatism, with Clarence Thomas as an originalist example. They explain binding versus persuasive precedent, unpublished opinions, and the federal court structure. They review Supreme Court overrulings (Plessy v. Ferguson and Brown v. Board, Booth/Payne v. Tennessee, Roper v. Simmons, Bush v. Gore, Roe v. Wade and Dobbs). The episode ends with listener mail about the sitcom two-parter, and Josh promises a future episode on the shadow docket.

segments.title: Opening banter on law and precedent
segments.summary: Josh introduces the dry topic of legal precedent, noting how legal wording and stable law shape everyday life.

segments.title: Henry II and the origins of common law
segments.summary: Henry II in 1154 moves England toward a single common law, establishing trial by jury and circuit courts. The common law spreads to England's colonies including the US, and is contrasted with civil law.

segments.title: Stare decisis and Brandeis's dissent
segments.summary: Stare decisis, meaning let the decision stand, is defined. Justice Brandeis's 1932 dissent in Burnett v. Coronado Oil and Gas says it is more important that the rule of law be settled than settled correctly, while bad decisions can still be overturned.
topics: Burnett v. Coronado Oil and Gas

segments.title: Factors for overturning precedent
segments.summary: The hosts list considerations for overturning precedent: constitutional versus statutory basis, workability, reliance (Miranda as an example), abandonment (Lawrence v. Texas), legitimacy, closeness of the vote, quality of reasoning, and changed facts.

segments.title: Originalism versus pragmatism
segments.summary: The hosts describe originalism, with Clarence Thomas as an example, and pragmatism. They discuss the tension between civil law and common law roles for judges and state their own middle-of-the-road views.

segments.title: Binding and persuasive precedent, federal courts
segments.summary: Binding authority is explained: state courts follow higher state courts, and federal courts are structured in circuits and districts, with the Supreme Court as final arbiter. Persuasive and unpublished opinions are non-binding.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of overruled precedents.

segments.title: Famous Supreme Court overrulings
segments.summary: The Supreme Court has overruled itself over 230 times, with most since Pollock v. Farmers' Loan and Trust. Examples discussed: Plessy v. Ferguson overturned by Brown v. Board of Education; Payne v. Tennessee allowing victim impact statements; Roper v. Simmons barring death sentences for minors; Bush v. Gore and its limiting language; Roe v. Wade overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization.

segments.title: Listener mail on sitcom episodes
segments.summary: Listeners wrote about the sitcom two-parter, correcting that Rhoda was a Mary Tyler Moore spinoff and not All in the Family and noting the Maggie Simpson omission. A listener praised the episode as a sleep aid.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the contact email, and promise a shadow docket short stuff episode.
